newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Redland sale talks lift share price.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Redland sale talks lift share price.

text.p: British building materials group Redland said on Thursday it was in talks with buyers for its French aggregates business in a bid to improve shareholder value after bad weather, sluggish European markets and a strong pound hit its 1996 results.

Redland chief executive Robert Napier told Reuters the company was in "in active discussions with a number of interested parties" on the sale of its loss-making French unit Granulats, which has a book value of 310 million pounds ($505 million).
News of the planned disposal was welcomed by the market and Redland shares soared 19 pence to 372.5p before edging back to 358p by 1310 GMT.
Analysts said the sale was a step in the right direction for Redland.
"The potential disposal of the French business is more likely than thought initially and the proceeds will allow Redland to develop the group," Arend Dickers of Salomon Brothers told Reuters.

One market-maker added: "The French operations were always something of a problem and it's positive news that they're getting rid of them. That's been the real good news today." Granulats, with 2,500 employees, has suffered from cuts and delays in public spending on infrastructure projects. Volume falls and price pressures in ready-mixed concrete resulted in an eight million pound loss.
This contributed to Redland's 1996 profits to fall to 259.1 million pounds, before exceptionals, down from 273.2 million in 1995.

After accounting for a one-off hit of 58 million pounds to account for goodwill related to the purchase of its Steetley subsidiary in 1992, Redland's profits fell to 200.9 million pounds. Sales dropped to 2.37 billion versus 2.50 billion, with the year dividend frozen at 16.67 pence per share.
Mark Hake, analyst at UBS, said some in the market had more negative expectations and were relieved to see results on track.

The profit fallback, despite a strong U.S. aggregates performance, was blamed by the company on bad weather in Europe last winter, sluggish German and French markets and the strong pound, which knocked seven million pounds off operating profits in 1996.
Napier said that if sterling remained at current levels through 1997, profits could suffer by 25 million pounds.

News of the French sale talks follows intense speculation over recent months on whether Redland was planning to spin off part or all its aggregates business. But the company remains committed to retaining its successful U.S. aggregates arm alongside the main European Roofing business RBB.
"The sale of the French aggregates leaves us with the European roofing division and a strong and successful U.S. aggregates division plus an improving UK business," Napier said.
Commenting on the outlook for the RBB roofing business in Germany, he said building permit numbers have stabilised.
"So in 1997 we should see a flat or only slightly declining market."
Price rises, plus lower variable costs meant "overall the Deutsche mark profits will be at least the same in 1997 despite a fall in volumes."
Salomon's Dickers said he was more upbeat about prospects for German housing than Redland.
The group plans to expand its RBB operations in eastern Europe and said regional sales should rise 20 percent this year after 25 percent East European growth in 1996.
It also plans to spend $40-50 million on bolt-on acquisitions in the U.S. aggregates business, Napier said. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
